reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it compares cloud-mining services and demonstrates the speaker's own hashpower purchases, account pages and contract terms. It includes claimed annual return figures and recommends buying capacity, but those claims are part of a service comparison; the supplied material does not establish that any listed operator is fraudulent or that the presenter diverts viewer funds.

opening.argument: The video ties paid mining participation directly to recurring income claims. The speaker says he buys mining power daily, proposes buying 500 gigahash every day, and describes annual income of 30–40%. He also tells viewers to buy capacity and cryptocurrency, then links that action to increased money value. This is not merely a neutral description: the requested purchase is presented alongside an ongoing mining-income opportunity.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a comparison does not remove the commercial call to action. The speaker explicitly says he will leave a link, describes buying power every day, and reports annual income figures. The material therefore does more than identify services: it connects directing viewers to a site and purchasing capacity with prospective returns.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The footage shows a walkthrough of accounts and contracts, but those screens do not establish that the speaker is promising viewers a guaranteed or recurring return. The stated figures are presented as claims about services, while the speaker's own purchases show only what he says he did, not that viewers were asked to transfer funds to him.

citations.quote: Because there are 30-40% of annual income

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: crypto-denominated payments, purchased hashing capacity, repeated daily investment, and unusually high return language. The speaker describes putting money into capacity every day, says a service has 30–40% annual income and even 45% annually, and presents a mining contract with BTC cost, hashing power and income fields. Framing these signals as an ordinary opportunity can make a speculative paid-mining offer appear more dependable than the evidence warrants.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The comparison framing does not neutralize the warning signs. A linked cloud-mining site is paired with daily purchases, crypto deposits and prominent percentage claims. Showing multiple services and account screens may increase credibility, but it does not supply audited proof that the advertised returns are realistic or sustainable.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: High percentages and crypto terminology are risk factors, not proof of fraud. The supplied evidence shows the speaker discussing services and displaying operational pages, including contract information; it does not show a guaranteed return, fabricated result, or loss suffered by a participant. The claim remains unverified, but unverified is not the same as deceptive.

opening.argument: The apparent tutorial functions as promotion because the speaker repeatedly presents specific services, explains how much capacity he buys, directs viewers to a cloud-mining site, and encourages further purchases. He says viewers should buy capacity and cryptocurrency and describes mining as profitable. Account pages, rankings, contract screens and balances give the recommendation an operational appearance, but the overall effect is to steer viewers toward paid mining participation rather than simply explain technology.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The operational demonstrations are precisely what make the promotion persuasive. A tutorial can still be promotional when it names services, supplies a link, explains repeated purchases and concludes that mining is profitable. The reference description understates this steering by treating the same demonstrations as neutral comparison evidence.

citations.quote: I will leave a link to this site to bitcoin cloud mining in the description.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The speaker's recommendation and demonstrations can support an educational or review role without proving a scam. The supplied pages show service interfaces and the speaker's discussion of his own activity, but they do not show that viewers must pay him, that he controls the services, or that the displayed figures guarantee income. Promotion-like language alone does not establish deception.
